intro.why: Monte Carlo methods are the first truly model-free RL methods: they learn values only from experienced episodes. Their strengths (no model, no bootstrapping bias) and weaknesses (waiting for episode ends, high variance) motivate TD learning in M8.

symbols: minimum exploration probability in ε-soft policies

sections.title: Estimation by random sampling
sections.plain: When something is hard to compute, sample it many times and average.
sections.body:
A Monte Carlo method is any algorithm that estimates a quantity by repeated random sampling: estimating π by throwing darts at a square, pricing options by simulating price paths, rendering light by tracing random rays. In RL the hard quantity is a state's value, $v_\pi(s) = \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s]$, and the samples are the returns actually received when the policy runs.

DP needed the model; MC needs only experience: sample sequences of states, actions and rewards, from real interaction or a simulator that can generate sample transitions (much easier to build than full probability tables).

MC applies to episodic tasks, because the return is known only once the episode ends. Classic MC is therefore an offline, episode-by-episode method: values and policies change only at episode boundaries.

sections.title: First-visit and every-visit MC prediction
sections.plain: Average the returns observed after visiting a state, counting either the first visit per episode or all of them.
sections.body:
First-visit MC prediction (estimating V ≈ v_π)
  1. Initialise V(s) arbitrarily; Returns(s) ← empty list for all s.
  2. Loop for each episode: generate S₀, A₀, R₁, …, S_{T−1}, A_{T−1}, R_T following π.
  3. G ← 0; for t = T−1 down to 0: G ← γG + R_{t+1}; unless Sₜ appears in S₀..S_{t−1}: append G to Returns(Sₜ); V(Sₜ) ← average(Returns(Sₜ)).

Every-visit MC drops the "unless" check and averages the returns after every occurrence. First-visit returns are independent, identically distributed estimates of $v_\pi(s)$, so by the law of large numbers the average converges with standard error falling as $1/\sqrt n$; every-visit is slightly biased within an episode but also converges to $v_\pi(s)$ as visits grow.

Estimates for different states are independent: MC does not bootstrap, so the cost of estimating one state's value does not depend on the number of states, which makes it attractive when only a few states matter.

sections.title: Worked example: a five-state grid world
sections.plain: Four recorded episodes, averaged state by state, give values with a revealing quirk.
sections.body:
States A–E; every move scores −1; exiting at D gives +10, exiting at A gives −10; $\gamma = 1$. Four episodes under a fixed policy, with first-visit returns (sum of rewards from that state to the end):

EpisodeTrajectory (state, reward)First-visit returns
1B −1, C −1, D +10B = 8, C = 9, D = 10
2B −1, C −1, D +10B = 8, C = 9, D = 10
3E −1, C −1, A −10E = −12, C = −11, A = −10
4E −1, C −1, D +10E = 8, C = 9, D = 10
$$V(A) = -10,\ V(B) = 8,\ V(C) = \tfrac{9+9-11+9}{4} = 4,\ V(D) = 10,\ V(E) = \tfrac{-12+8}{2} = -2$$

The quirk. B and E both move into C, yet $V(B) = 8$ and $V(E) = -2$. Direct MC ignores the fact that they share a successor; each state is learned in isolation from the episodes that happened to pass through it. With the model (or with bootstrapping) both would be tied to $V(C)$: $-1 + 4 = 3$. MC agrees only in the limit of infinite data.

Strengths: simple, model-free, no propagated bias from other estimates, provably convergent, robust to non-Markov states. Weaknesses: wastes transition structure, needs many visits per state, high variance, must wait for episode ends.

sections.title: Incremental and constant-step-size updates
sections.plain: Update the running average after each episode; or use a fixed step to track change.
sections.body:
$$V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \frac{1}{N(S_t)}\big[G_t - V(S_t)\big]\qquad\text{or}\qquad V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[G_t - V(S_t)\big]$$

The first form reproduces the sample average without storing returns (C's returns 9, 9, −11, 9 give 9, 9, 2.33, 4). The second, constant-α MC, forgets old episodes and suits nonstationary problems. Both have the familiar form old + step × (target − old), with target $G_t$, the actual return. TD (M8) will replace this target with $R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})$.

sections.title: Monte Carlo control with action values
sections.plain: Estimate Q from returns, act greedily on it, repeat: GPI without a model.
sections.body:
Without a model, state values are not enough to choose actions (a one-step lookahead needs $p$). So MC control estimates action values $q_\pi(s,a)$, averaging returns after visits to $(s,a)$, and improves by acting greedily:

$$\pi(s) \leftarrow \arg\max_a Q(s,a)$$

This is GPI: evaluation by averaging returns (episode by episode, not to convergence), improvement by greedification. By the policy improvement theorem each greedy step is at least as good, provided evaluation is accurate enough.

The exploration problem. With a deterministic policy, many state–action pairs are never visited, so their returns are never observed and their Q-values never improve. Exploration must be maintained.

sections.title: Exploring starts and ε-soft policies
sections.plain: Start episodes from random state–action pairs, or never let any action's probability drop to zero.
sections.body:
Exploring starts (ES): every episode begins with a randomly chosen state–action pair, with all pairs having non-zero probability. Then MC ES alternates evaluation and greedy improvement after each episode. It is easy in simulation (deal any blackjack hand) but often impossible in the real world (a robot always starts at its dock).

ε-soft on-policy control: keep $\pi(a\mid s) \ge \varepsilon/|\mathcal A(s)|$ for all actions. With ε-greedy improvement:

$$\pi(a\mid s) = \begin{cases}1-\varepsilon+\varepsilon/|\mathcal A(s)| & a = \arg\max_{a'}Q(s,a')\\ \varepsilon/|\mathcal A(s)| & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

The policy improvement theorem still holds within the class of ε-soft policies, so this converges to the best ε-soft policy, slightly worse than the optimal deterministic one because it never stops exploring.

sections.title: On-policy vs off-policy learning
sections.plain: Learn about the policy you follow, or learn about a different one from someone else's behaviour.
sections.body:
On-policy methods evaluate and improve the policy used to make decisions (e.g. ε-soft MC control). Off-policy methods learn about a target policy $\pi$ (often greedy) from data generated by a behaviour policy $b$ (exploratory, or logged from humans or older systems).

Coverage: every action $\pi$ might take must have $b(a\mid s) > 0$. The mismatch is corrected by the importance-sampling ratio:

$$\rho_{t:T-1} = \prod_{k=t}^{T-1}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{b(A_k\mid S_k)}$$

The unknown transition probabilities cancel in this ratio, so it needs no model. Ordinary IS, $V(s) = \sum\rho G/N(s)$, is unbiased but can have enormous (even infinite) variance; weighted IS, $V(s) = \sum\rho G/\sum\rho$, is biased (bias vanishes with data) but has much lower variance and is preferred in practice. Off-policy MC control walks each episode backwards with a cumulative weight and stops when the behaviour action is not the greedy one. M7 develops all of this in depth.

sections.title: Blackjack
sections.plain: A card game where MC shines: easy to simulate, hard to model.
sections.body:
Goal: card sum as close to 21 as possible without exceeding it; face cards count 10, an ace counts 1 or 11 (a usable ace counts 11 without busting). Player hits or sticks; dealer then hits below 17. Reward +1 win, 0 draw, −1 loss; $\gamma = 1$, so returns equal the final reward.

State: player sum (12–21), dealer's showing card (A–10), usable ace or not: 200 states. Below 12 the player always hits.

Computing $p(s',r\mid s,a)$ for blackjack is tedious (it depends on the dealer's whole future draw), yet generating sample games is trivial: MC's sweet spot. Code example ex2: under "stick only on 20 or 21", states with sums 12–19 against a dealer 10 are worth about −0.56 to −0.75, while 20 and 21 are worth +0.44 and +0.89. ε-soft MC control (400,000 hands) learns a policy close to the known basic strategy: stick on 17+, stick on 13–16 against a dealer 2–6, hit against 7–A; cells near the boundary remain noisy.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• MC is unbiased but slow. Variance grows with episode length and stochasticity; in long tasks TD or n-step methods usually win.
  • MC tree search (M13) uses the same principle: random rollouts to estimate the value of a position.
  • Policy gradients such as REINFORCE (M11) are Monte Carlo methods for the policy: they use full returns, with the same variance issues and the same fix (baselines).
  • Off-policy evaluation in industry (recommendation, ads, healthcare) relies on importance sampling with logged propensities; weighted and doubly-robust estimators are standard.

code.title: Monte Carlo estimation: darts and the five-state grid world
code.explain: Estimates π with 10² to 10⁶ darts, then computes first-visit returns and values for the four grid-world episodes, both as batch averages and incrementally.
mistakes: Counting the same state twice in first-visit MC.
Computing returns forwards from the start of the episode.
code.notes: The incremental and batch averages agree exactly.
code.code:
"""Monte Carlo = estimate by averaging random samples.

1) Estimate pi by throwing random darts at a square.
2) First-visit MC prediction on a five-state grid world from four observed episodes (gamma = 1).
3) The same estimates computed incrementally: V <- V + (1/N)(G - V).
"""
import random
random.seed(0)
for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    inside = sum(1 for _ in range(n) if random.random() ** 2 + random.random() ** 2 <= 1)
    print(f"pi estimate with {n:>9,} darts: {4 * inside / n:.4f}")

episodes = [[("B", -1), ("C", -1), ("D", 10)],
            [("B", -1), ("C", -1), ("D", 10)],
            [("E", -1), ("C", -1), ("A", -10)],
            [("E", -1), ("C", -1), ("D", 10)]]
returns = {}
V, N = {}, {}
for ep in episodes:
    G, rets = 0.0, []
    for s, r in reversed(ep):              # gamma = 1: return = sum of rewards from here to the end
        G = r + G; rets.append((s, G))
    rets.reverse(); seen = set()
    for s, G in rets:
        if s in seen: continue             # first visit only
        seen.add(s); returns.setdefault(s, []).append(G)
        N[s] = N.get(s, 0) + 1; V[s] = V.get(s, 0.0) + (G - V.get(s, 0.0)) / N[s]   # incremental mean
print("\nfirst-visit returns per state:", {s: returns[s] for s in sorted(returns)})
print("V (batch average):  ", {s: sum(g) / len(g) for s, g in sorted(returns.items())})
print("V (incremental):    ", {s: round(V[s], 3) for s in sorted(V)})
print("B and E both lead to C, yet V(B) = 8 and V(E) = -2: MC learns each state only from its own episodes.")
